steps.title: Problem overview and goals
steps.content:
Design a Price Alert System that allows users to set alerts for products and notifies them when prices drop below their target. The system must support near real-time monitoring, handle millions of alerts and products, and deliver notifications through multiple channels (email, SMS, app).

Key goals include:
- Scalability to millions of users and alerts
- Low-latency price monitoring and alerting
- Accurate and reliable notification delivery
- Efficient price tracking from multiple sources (polling, webhooks, vendor feeds)
- Cost-effective operations and maintainability
- Security and privacy for user data
- Observability for troubleshooting and performance monitoring

This system is critical for e-commerce and financial platforms where timely price information drives user engagement and revenue. It must be resilient to failures, easy to operate, and extensible for future notification channels or alert types.

steps.title: User journeys & API surface
steps.content:
Primary user journeys:
1. A user browses products and sets a price alert specifying a target price or percentage drop, and preferred notification channel.
2. The system continuously monitors prices from multiple sources, updating the product catalog and cache.
3. When a price drop matches an alert, the system triggers a notification via the user's chosen channel (email, SMS, app push).
4. Users can view, update, or delete their alerts, and review price history for products.

API endpoints:
- POST /alerts: Create a new alert (requires authentication, input validation)
- GET /alerts: List user alerts
- DELETE /alerts/{id}: Remove an alert
- GET /products/{id}/price-history: Retrieve price history for a product

The API must support versioning, error handling, and rate limiting to prevent abuse. It should also provide clear error messages and documentation for developers integrating with the system.

properties.description: HTTP API for users to create, view, and delete price alerts. Implements structured logging, distributed tracing, health checks, and circuit breaker patterns for downstream failures. Enforces RBAC authorization, rate limiting, and encryption at rest for all alert data. Supports feature flags for safe deployment of new logic. Designed for horizontal scalability, auto-scaling, and high availability.

steps.title: Add the Alert Service
steps.content: Centralizes alert logic: matching price drops, deduplication, and notification orchestration. All alert data is encrypted at rest. RBAC ensures only authorized users can manage alerts. Health checks and auto-scaling maximize reliability. Feature flags enable safe experimentation.

component.highlightReason: Stores product metadata, price history, and alert associations.

properties.description: Stores product details, price history, and alert associations. Supports efficient queries for price lookups and alert matching. Implements connection pooling, aggressive caching, cache warming, query optimization, and backup strategies for reliability and performance. Provides audit trails for price changes and alert mappings. All sensitive data is encrypted at rest. Uses read replicas to improve performance and reliability under heavy load. Recommended to use a managed database service for cost efficiency and operational simplicity.

steps.title: Add the Product Catalog DB

This table contains user identifiers, authentication hashes, and structured preference blobs consumed by the Alert Service to personalize notifications. Index email for fast lookup, encrypt sensitive fields at rest, and apply strict RBAC and audit logging for access. Designed for high read availability using read replicas and caching for session/profile queries.

Optimized for fast price lookups and joins with alert evaluation: index id and sku, consider materialized views for common queries, and keep recent price in a cache for low-latency alerts. Support denormalized fields for common filters and well-defined migration paths for schema changes.

steps.title: Alert matching and notification trade-offs
steps.content:
Designing an effective alert matching and notification system for a price alert platform involves navigating several key trade-offs. First, there is the choice between batch and real-time evaluation. Batch processing can be more cost-effective and easier to scale for low-priority or bulk alerts, but it introduces latency, which may not be acceptable for high-value or time-sensitive notifications. Real-time evaluation, on the other hand, ensures users are notified almost instantly when their alert conditions are met, but it requires more resources and careful engineering to maintain low latency and high throughput under heavy load.

Deduplication is another critical concern. Without robust deduplication logic, users may receive multiple notifications for the same price drop, leading to notification fatigue and a poor user experience. Implementing deduplication requires tracking recent notifications, correlating them with alert triggers, and applying rules to suppress redundant messages.

Balancing notification latency with system load is also essential. Spikes in price changes or user activity can overwhelm the system, causing delays or dropped notifications. To address this, the system should employ rate limiting, backpressure mechanisms, and circuit breaker patterns to gracefully degrade service under load and prevent cascading failures.

Finally, integrating a service mesh can help manage traffic, enforce policies, and provide observability across microservices. This enables fine-grained control over alert evaluation and notification delivery, supporting both reliability and scalability.

steps.title: Scaling, caching, and rate limiting
steps.content: To ensure the Price Alert System can handle millions of users and alerts efficiently, several scaling, caching, and rate limiting strategies must be employed. Sharding alert evaluation by product or user is a foundational approach, allowing the workload to be distributed across multiple servers or processing nodes. This not only improves throughput but also isolates failures, so that issues affecting one shard do not impact the entire system. Caching hot prices—those that are frequently queried or updated—reduces the load on the primary database and accelerates alert evaluation. An in-memory cache like Redis can store recent price data, enabling rapid lookups and minimizing latency for both alert matching and user-facing queries. Cache invalidation strategies must be carefully designed to ensure data consistency, especially when new price data is ingested or when alerts are triggered. Rate limiting is crucial for protecting the system from abuse and ensuring fair usage across all users and channels. By applying rate limits per user, per channel, or even per IP address, the system can prevent spam, avoid overloading notification channels, and maintain a high quality of service. Monitoring notification volume and alerting on spikes helps operators detect unusual activity or potential abuse early. Finally, optimizing the Product Catalog DB with connection pooling and query optimization techniques ensures that even under heavy load, the database remains responsive. Indexing, query tuning, and horizontal scaling of the database layer further contribute to the system’s overall scalability and reliability. Edge Cases & Failure Handling: Each component should document how it handles edge cases such as network partitions, database failover, cache invalidation failures, and message queue backpressure. For example, the Notification Worker should specify retry logic and fallback channels for undeliverable messages. The Alert Service should describe how it handles duplicate or conflicting alerts. The Monitoring Service should outline alerting thresholds for system anomalies and escalation procedures for persistent failures.

steps.title: MVP implementation plan
steps.content: Stage 1: Build Alert API + Service, wire Product DB and Price Ingestion, and support basic email notifications. Stage 2: Add cache and notification queue. Stage 3: Implement Notification Worker, DLQ, and multi-channel support. Stage 4: Add monitoring, rate limiting, and scale testing. Integrate structured logging, distributed tracing, and dashboards from the start.

Provides APIs for updating notification channels, alert thresholds, and privacy settings. Integrates with Alert API and Notification Worker for personalized experiences. Implements strong RBAC access controls and encryption for user data at rest. Health checks ensure service reliability. Centralizes all user-related data for maintainability and extensibility.

properties.description: Implements mTLS, traffic routing, circuit breaking, and distributed telemetry. Enhances security and observability for service-to-service communication and integrates with existing monitoring. Provides platform-level policies for retries, load balancing, and canary routing, reducing developer burden and centralizing operational controls. Enables consistent telemetry and tracing context propagation across services to improve incident response and performance analysis.

component.highlightReason: Edge caching for UI and static resources to reduce latency and backend load.
component.label: CDN (CloudFront/Cloudflare)

properties.description: Edge caching for static assets (UI, images, JS), TLS termination, origin shielding, and geo-distribution. Reduces backend load and improves performance. Supports cache invalidation strategies, origin failover, and fine-grained caching rules per path or content-type. Integrates with CI for automated asset purging and provides security features like WAF and TLS termination to protect origin servers.

steps.title: Add CDN for static assets
steps.content: Serve UI and static assets from the edge to reduce backend load and latency. Configure cache-control headers and long TTLs for static assets.

connection.description: CDN forwards requests to the Alert API origin for dynamic endpoints and API traffic.
connection.label: CDN → Alert API

steps.title: CDN → Alert API (edge → origin)

component.highlightReason: Edge filtering, OWASP protections, and DDoS mitigation for public endpoints.
component.label: Web Application Firewall (WAF)

properties.description: WAF provides rule-based filtering, managed rulesets, bot mitigation, and DDoS protections at the edge. Place the WAF between the CDN and origin/API to block common web attacks (OWASP top 10) and to apply custom IP allow/deny lists. Integrate WAF logs with the Monitoring Service to surface suspicious traffic patterns and automate alerts. Configure managed rulesets, rate-limiting policies, and request inspection to stop malicious requests before they reach backend services.

steps.title: Add the Web Application Firewall (WAF)
steps.content: Deploy a WAF at the edge to filter malicious requests and reduce attack surface. Integrate with the CDN and monitoring for automated blocking and alerting.

connection.label: WAF → Alert API

steps.title: WAF → Alert API (edge protection)
steps.content: Protect the public API by filtering harmful requests at the edge via the WAF.
